Whether a skill earns its place at all is a fleet-shaped question: never loading in one repo may only mean it isn't that repo's subject, while never loading in **any** of them means the trigger is mis-described — or that the content should never have been gated behind a skill in the first place. Only a view across every member separates those.

The **conformance checks** are carried at the same grain and for exactly the same reason, and they answer a sharper question, because a check failure is an observed correction rather than an inferred one: the finding went back into the session and the agent fixed it before the work left the branch. A rule with steady failures across the fleet is a guard earning its keep; a rule that has never fired in *any* member is unreachable or describing something that does not happen; a rule firing on nearly every run is a default the corpus should change rather than a violation worth blocking on. The `errors` counter reads differently from all three — enforcement was silently off — and is the one number here whose right value is zero.

The grain is therefore full — week × repo × skill, and week × repo × rule, for history, plus each member's current day window verbatim — with nothing pre-summed. Every coarser view stays derivable from the file; a summary that threw the grain away would not.

A member still on an older fold carries no `checks` key. It lands as an empty check row, never as an exception: the sweep leads the members' upgrades, so that is the normal state for a while.

## Coverage gaps are reported, not skipped

A covered member with no usage file (not folding yet), or one whose file cannot be read, is listed in `coverage.absent` with the reason — census-style. A denominator with an invisible hole in it is worse than no denominator at all.

The `coverage` section accounts for the **whole fleet**, not just the members: uncovered repos land under `coverage.uncovered` and archived/fork/excluded ones under `coverage.outOfScope` (reason inline), neither contributing to any number. The worker also emits a run summary on **every** run — even one that opens no PR — naming every repo under its state, and flagging the folding members with no captured activity that day (*inactive today*). That daily fact lives in the run report, not the file: it moves with the date alone, and the file's unchanged-compare deliberately ignores the day stamp so an unmoved fleet opens no PR.

## A dormant member leaves the denominator

A member that declares `"dormant": true` ([the scheduler's gate](../../../claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)) is dropped from every rate and listed under `coverage.dormant` — distinct from `coverage.absent`, because "not in the race" and "should be folding and isn't" are different facts. Averaging a deliberately silent repo in would drag every fleet-wide number toward zero as the fleet accumulates finished projects. The test is `isDormant`, re-exported from the engine, so the sweep and the member's own scheduler cannot disagree.

## It is a sample, not a census

The file carries a `_note` saying so. Its whole population is *captured* sessions: sessions that merged, plus sessions that ended cleanly enough for the SessionEnd capture to fire. A session whose container was reclaimed, or that crashed, is invisible to every number in it.

The check counts sit inside a narrower boundary still, and the note says that too: they are what a *session* saw. A CI run counts when the session pulled its job log in — which is what "the agent was in the loop on it" means, and it is the loop that produces the correction — while a nightly or post-merge run nobody looked at does not, because nothing was corrected. CI can only see a run that *printed* something, so its share rides separately as `ciRuns`/`ciFailures` rather than skewing a rate. The under-count is one-directional — every check number is a floor on activations, never an over-count — which is what keeps "the checks caught N things fleet-wide this week" a claim worth making.

## Not a fleet mechanism

Its *implementation* reads every repo under the owner, but its declaration, scheduling and lifecycle are those of **any pack task**: it is active because this repo declares the `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` pack, and it runs on this repo's ordinary scheduler. It declares no `fleet` signal and no `fleet` session scope — the cross-repo reach lives in the implementation, never in the wiring.

1	// claudinite-growth task: usage-fold — the per-repo skill-usage aggregate
2	// (skill-usage-metrics DESIGN §5). `agent_model: 'none'` with
3	// `code_work: 'node worker.mjs'`: the whole pass is deterministic code the
4	// executor runs as code-work — no agent phase, seconds of runtime.
5	//
6	// WHY: a skill is MOUNTED per repo, but mounting only puts a name and a one-line
7	// description into the session prompt — actually LOADING it is model discretion, and
8	// nothing recorded whether it ever happened. The only evidence is the session
9	// transcript, which is ephemeral and dies at retention on the logs branch. So the
10	// promotion ladder's skill-vs-prose call had no empirical feedback: a skill whose
11	// trigger never fires looked exactly like one that fires daily. This task counts
12	// loads — and the DENOMINATORS that make a count mean something — out of the logs
13	// this repo already captures, into a small tracked aggregate.
14	//
15	// It also counts what the SCHEDULER did: per task, how many runs dispatched an agent,
16	// how many were deterministic preprocessing only, how many its precondition skipped,
17	// how many failed, how many were deferred. Those come from the scheduler's own run
18	// records in its Actions logs — a census of scheduled work, beside the sample of
19	// captured sessions everything else here is drawn from.
20	//
21	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
22	
23	export default {
24	  id: 'usage-fold',
25	  frequency: 'daily',                    // day rows are the unit; a day closes once
26	  precondition_signals: ['conversationLogs'],
27	  agent_model: 'none',                   // pure code — no agent (task-code-work DESIGN §4)
28	  expected_outcome: 'merged-pr',         // the regenerated GENERATED aggregate rides a PR landed per the repo's delivery settings
29	  code_work: 'node worker.mjs',
30	  // One tree read plus one blob read per capture file in the ~10-day window, all
31	  // local git, then one PR. A busy repo captures a few files a day, so this is
32	  // seconds; 600s is ~100x that, generous enough that a huge backlog on a first fold
33	  // still completes while a hung run is killed well inside the hourly cadence.
34	  code_work_timeout: 600,
35	
36	  // Always runs. Deliberately NOT gated on fresh captures, nor on the logs branch
37	  // existing at all: the fold has two sources, and the second one — the scheduler's
38	  // own task-run records — exists in any repo that has a scheduler, including one
39	  // whose sessions are all unattended and captured nothing. Its job also includes
40	  // advancing the week watermark past days that have closed, which is true on a
41	  // quiet repo too. A run with nothing new recomputes to a byte-identical file and
42	  // opens no PR, so a wasted run costs seconds and produces no noise.
43	  precondition(signals) {
44	    const logs = signals.conversationLogs ?? {};
45	    const captured = logs.present === true
46	      ? `${logs.logCount ?? 0} captured log(s)`
47	      : 'no conversation-logs branch yet (task-run records only)';
48	    return { run: true, reason: `fold ${captured} into the usage aggregate (day rows recomputed, closed days folded into their week)` };
49	  },
50	};
51

1	// claudinite-fleet-sheepdog task: fleet-usage — the fleet-wide skill-usage aggregate, as a scheduled
2	// task. `agent_model: 'none'` with `code_work: 'node worker.mjs'`: the
3	// whole pass is deterministic code the executor runs as code-work — no agent
4	// phase. The worker calls its sibling, the sweep
5	// (aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs): read every member's own usage aggregate and rebuild
6	// this repo's `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` as a pure function of them.
7	//
8	// WHY: every member folds its OWN skill-usage numbers, and can therefore answer "does
9	// this skill ever load HERE". The question the promotion ladder actually asks — does
10	// a skill earn its place at all — is fleet-shaped: never loading in one repo may just
11	// mean it isn't that repo's subject, while never loading in ANY of them means the
12	// trigger is mis-described or the content should never have been gated behind a skill.
13	// Only something looking at every member at once can tell those apart.
14	//
15	// CLASSIFICATION (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §6, the same note the census and the
16	// freshness sweep carry): an ORDINARY PACK TASK, not a fleet mechanism. Its
17	// *implementation* reads every member over a PAT, but its declaration, scheduling and
18	// lifecycle are exactly those of any pack task — it is active because this repo
19	// declares the claudinite-fleet-sheepdog pack, and it runs however this repo's tasks run. Hence no
20	// `fleet` signal, and no session scope of its own (the PACK declares the executor
21	// reach — session-scope.mjs): those describe how a task is WIRED,
22	// and nothing about this task's wiring is fleet-shaped.
23	//
24	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
25	
26	export default {
27	  id: 'fleet-usage',
28	  frequency: 'daily',                    // the members fold daily; this follows them
29	  precondition_signals: [],              // no signal — the sweep reads the fleet itself, over the PAT
30	  agent_model: 'none',                   // pure code — no agent (task-code-work DESIGN §4)
31	  expected_outcome: 'merged-pr',         // the regenerated GENERATED aggregate rides a PR landed per the repo's delivery settings
32	  code_work: 'node worker.mjs',
33	  // One paged enumeration plus two REST reads per member (the coverage probe and the

# Writing migration and implementation plans

A plan's phases are not a narrative of the work; they are a **schedule of who has to be present
when**. Ordering them by topic — "phase 1: the store, phase 2: the workers, phase 3: cutover" —
scatters the moments that need a human across the whole run, and every one of them stops it. Order
them by *what blocks*, and the run ends with a stretch nobody has to attend.

Everything below assumes the change is already agreed: the problem, and that this migration is the
right way to solve it (basics' *Starting any requested change*). The end-state's **shape** —
converging in one forced pass, accepting legacy input at the door, a standing mechanism for
stragglers — is [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Planning a migration*; this skill is the ordering.

## Two deliverables, two homes — and only two

An initiative produces at most one document and one issue, and neither may do the
other's job:

- **The design doc** (`docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md`, where the project keeps one)
  describes the **end state and its rationale** — what the mechanism is once the
  work is done, and why that shape over the alternatives, with each alternative's
  drawbacks stated. It never carries the previous state as narrative, the requests
  or conversation that led here, owner attributions or opinions, progress, or a
  phase list. The test: a reader who arrives after the migration finishes must
  find nothing to delete. Legacy shapes appear only where the end state itself
  keeps handling them (a decode map, an accepted input) — as mechanism, not as
  history.
- **The migration is work, not a document.** Its plan lives in the tracking issue
  and nowhere else — never a plan or migration document committed to the repo. A
  plan document goes stale the moment work starts and cannot be checked off; the
  issue is checkable, append-only, and dies with the work.

## The three blocks, and where each belongs

Sort every step of the plan into one of three kinds, and let that sort — not the subject matter —
decide the phase it lands in.

**1. Out-of-band setup — before any code changes.** Anything performed outside the repo that a
later step will need: provisioning an environment, creating a session or runner, setting a secret
or variable, granting a permission, flipping a platform setting, registering a webhook. Nearly all
of it is **non-destructive** — it adds a capability that nothing yet consumes, so doing it early
costs nothing and changes no behaviour. Doing it *late* costs the whole run: the plan reaches the
step that reads the secret and stops until someone is available.

Front-load all of it into phase zero, before the first line of code. Write it as its own issue
with a checkbox per step (basics' *Handing over a human-only step*), stating for each what stays
broken while it is off. And before writing it down, confirm you genuinely cannot do it yourself —
a step handed to a human that you could have taken is the most expensive kind of block there is.

The exception is the genuinely destructive step — deleting the old store, revoking the old
credential, removing the compatibility shim. Those are not setup; they are the migration's tail,
and they belong after the cutover has been observed working — which is **not** a later phase. A
cleanup phase falls due long after the run that would have done it ended, and nothing brings it
back. File it as work that comes back on its own (basics' *Spotting a change that should wait*),
in the same change that creates the thing it cleans up, naming what closes it and what to remove.
Then the owner can forget about it, which is the point.

**2. Review and authorization gates — collapsed into one pass.** Every phase that ships code is a
gate: the owner must read it and approve it before the next phase can start. A plan with four
coding phases has four such waits, and each one is dead time whose length nobody controls.

Write **all** the code first, as a stack of PRs each based on the previous, and put the whole
stack in front of the owner together. The stack keeps the reviewable units small and independent —
one concern per PR, as ever — while costing one arrival of attention rather than four. Merge it
base-first once approved.

Approval of the stack is approval of the stack: it does not extend to a fix authored afterwards
(basics' *Acting on an approval to merge, ship or proceed*).

**3. Execution steps — whatever is left.** Once phase zero has landed the setup and the stack has
merged, the remaining steps run the migration: force the converge, backfill the members, watch the
cutover, retire the shim. If the first two sorts were done properly there is no gate among them —
they can be run at will, in one sitting, by whoever is at the keyboard.

That is the test of the plan. **Read the phases in order and mark every point where the run would
have to stop and wait for a person.** Each mark that falls after phase zero and the review pass is
a step that was sorted wrong. Move it, or say in the plan why it genuinely cannot move.

## Writing it down

- **The plan is a tracking issue**, and the phases are its checkboxes. Status and remaining work
  live there; a design document, where the project keeps one, carries the mechanism and not the
  progress.
- **Each phase names its exit condition**, observable and stated as a thing that reads back true —
  not "cutover done" but "every member's stamp shows the new ref". A phase whose end is a judgment
  call is a phase that stays open.
- **Nothing closes on a human's memory.** A step you cannot verify now gets a mechanism that comes
  to you — a scheduled task, a watched PR, an issue something converges (basics' *When verifying now
  is genuinely impossible*). A phase whose closing condition is "check next week" is not a phase.
- **Size each step to what it is**, and don't restate in the plan what the design document or the
  linked issue already carries.

## Working through the plan

Once the plan is agreed, the issue body's plan is **append-only**. While implementing, scheduler run its
checkboxes and add below it — a comment, or a new section for what the work turned up — and never
edit, reword, condense or re-order what was already there.

The body is the record of what was agreed, and it is the only copy: an edit overwrites it in place
with nothing left to diff against, so a plan silently rewritten to match what was built reads
afterwards as a plan that was followed. Keeping it fixed is what makes the divergence visible —
and a divergence is the interesting part, not an embarrassment to tidy away.

So when the work shows a phase was wrong, say so **underneath**: what the plan assumed, what turned
out to be true, and what you did instead. If that changes the plan going forward, the new steps are
an addition, appended and dated; the superseded ones stay where they are, marked superseded rather
than deleted.

The exception is a **correction to the plan itself before implementation of it starts** — the owner
saying the plan misreads what they asked for. That is a correction (basics' *Acting on a
correction*): repair the body, since there is no work yet for it to have diverged from.

## Reviewing someone else's plan

Run the same sort over it. The findings worth raising, in order of what they cost:

1. A secret, permission, environment or account created **after** code that depends on it.
2. More than one review gate — two or more phases that each end in "open a PR and wait".
3. A destructive step scheduled before the replacement has been observed working, or a
   cleanup written as a phase rather than filed as work that returns.
4. A phase with no stated exit condition, or one only a person can judge.
5. A step handed to a human that the agent could have performed itself.

input.title: claudinite-dashboard: usage-backed data plane, per-repo redesign, repo/fleet modes — and retire fleet-usage
input.body:
Tracking issue for the dashboard redesign. The plan below is ordered by what blocks (out-of-band setup → one review pass over a PR stack → unattended execution → destructive tail), not by subject. Once agreed, this body is append-only.

## First, the question asked: is `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` redundant?

**Yes — with one catch that sequences the removal.**

- The sweep is a **stateless full recompute, a pure function of the members' current files** (its own README says so). It holds **no longer history** than the members: each member's week rows are append-once and never pruned, so the member files are the complete record and the fleet file adds no depth.
- **Nothing in the canon reads it.** Grep finds only the task's own files, its tests, docs and the `.gitattributes` entry. It was built for fleet-wide analysis by a human/agent reading one file — the fleet dashboard is now that reader, better.
- The **access argument is real and favors dropping**: the aggregate in Shepherd shows anyone with Shepherd read the whole fleet's numbers, while the dashboard reads each member's file *as the viewer* — a repo you can't read renders "not visible to you". Per-repo files are the permission-correct source.
- **Catch 1 — it is currently the fleet dashboard's roster.** Shepherd's declaration reads `"rosterFile": "usage-fleet.GENERATED.json"`. The member list is the one thing genuinely fleet-shaped in it, so the fleet page needs a replacement roster source *before* the file goes (PR 3 below).
- Catch 2 — the `coverage` census (absent / dormant / out-of-scope, with reasons) is the only other content member files can't hold. The fleet page derives it live: a rostered repo with no readable usage file **is** the absent row, and `dormant` is read off the member's own declaration.

So: drop the task and the file — sequenced after the fleet page stops reading it (the tail, below).

## Design decisions

1. **Fresh vs past split.** *Fresh* per page load: repo metadata, head sha, the open-issue page, the runs list — all ETag-revalidated (a 304 is free), target **~5 requests warm, all 304s** on the per-repo page. *Past*: one blob read of `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`, cached by head sha — **zero requests while `main` is unmoved**. Nothing else reaches back in time over the API.
2. **usage.GENERATED.json v3 stays raw data**, not UI-shaped: per-hour and per-day series with per-item detail preserved, so future UI changes re-render without re-folding. Readers accept v2 (legacy at the door): an absent series renders as a stated gap, never a guessed zero — the #1001 rule.
3. **Freshness provenance**: a `generated` stamp in the file, excluded from the worker's unchanged-compare exactly as the fleet file's `generatedAt` already is — so it reads "when the data last moved" and a quiet repo still opens no PR. The head-commit date the page already holds is the upper bound beside it.
4. **usage-fold goes hourly, gated on movement** — signals `commits` + `conversationLogs` + runs movement; a quiet hour declines. The REST-read families stay incremental past their watermarks; day recomputes stay local-git and free.
5. **Mode is structural, no new config key**: a declaration with a roster source (`owner` or legacy `rosterFile`) is a **fleet-dashboard** deployment, anything else is a **repo-dashboard** one; `build-site.mjs` mounts that landing. Nothing to ask at adoption, nothing to misconfigure.
6. **Fleet roster = live enumeration as the viewer**: config `owner` (+ existing `exclude`), membership = a readable `.claudinite-checks.json` at head (sha-cached, so the probe is amortized). This also honors the standing "no repo list exists anywhere in canon code" decision. Fallback if enumeration proves too costly at fleet size: a slim `roster.GENERATED.json` from a Shepherd fleet task (the sanctioned daily auto-merged GENERATED-file shape) — not built unless measurement says so.

## Phase 0 — out-of-band, human

- [ ] Enable **Pages, source "GitHub Actions", on ClaudiniteCanary** — the one repository setting no Action can flip. The adoption run files its own handover issue there with the link; while off, only the deploy job fails. (Shepherd already deploys, so its setting is expected on — verified as an execution step, promoted here only if it turns out off.)

Sign-in for the fleet deployment is already tracked in #996 / #942 / #1003 and blocks nothing here — the token box works today.

## The stack — all code, one review pass, merged base-first

- [ ] **PR 1 — usage-fold v3** (the data plane; everything downstream renders from it)
  - **`hours` tier**, rolling ~72h keyed by UTC hour: counts of scheduler runs / executor runs / agentic runs, plus raw per-run entries (task ids evaluated / executed, which dispatched an agent, conclusion) so the UI can build hover detail. Folded from the Actions runs listing + the run records, incremental past `runsFoldedThrough`. This is the queue-era successor to the dead `tasks` census — closes #994.
  - **day-row additions**: `queue` — closed work items per task × outcome, appended past a watermark (settled data, never re-read); `ruleTokens` — sessions seen + rule tokens summed, parsed from the session-start summary line the capture logs already carry; `linesCommitted` — local git, free; `releases` — tags, one cheap read.
  - **aspirational, resolved inside this PR**: per-session token spend — probe the capture JSONL for usage records; carried if present, otherwise the README names it absent (a stated gap, not an approximation).
  - `generated` stamp per decision 3; `frequency: 'hourly'` + movement precondition per decision 4; README rewritten.
  - Exit: fold runs green on this repo's own logs; a v2 file re-folds to v3 without loss; a quiet-hour run declines.
- [ ] **PR 2 — per-repo page redesign**
  - **At-a-glance tiles**: stars, CI health, waiting-on-a-person minutes (the fleet's flat-rate constant, same published assumption note), "N parked for approval / M for a decision" (the park-kind split `summariseMember` already makes, reused per-repo), open PRs + issues, engine/pack drift vs `canonRepo` (reads *unknown* when unset — never guessed).
  - **One work table** replacing the tasks and queue tables: three views — **stuck / pending / all** — over the union of declared tasks and their items, with view-dependent columns; transitions FLIP-animated (rows enter/leave, columns slide; hand-rolled, the pack keeps zero dependencies). Blocked/parked rows always on top; healthy rows collapsed behind **show all**.
  - **Task execution summary**: per-day stacked outcome bars (the fleet's shape), from the usage `queue` series, today's partial day topped up from the live issue page already fetched.
  - **Scheduler-runs panel condensed to a 48h hourly stacked graph** — scheduler / executor / agentic per hour, hover naming the tasks evaluated / executed / agentic — from the usage `hours` tier, the freshest hours topped up from the runs list already fetched.
  - **Growth block, centrally placed**: 30-day graph, dual axes — rule tokens added to sessions per day, checks executed per day — plus the aspirational series where the file carries them.
  - Exit: cold/warm request counts measured and stated in the README, warm within the ~5-request target.
- [ ] **PR 3 — fleet page from member usage files**
  - Member rows and the activity/growth panels render from each member's usage file (sha-keyed read, zero when unmoved) plus a minimal fresh read per member (ETag'd open-issue page + repo meta), through the existing cache/budget tiers.
  - Roster from `owner` enumeration per decision 6; `rosterFile` still accepted so Shepherd's current declaration keeps working until flipped.
  - A rostered member with no usage file renders **"not folding yet"** — the coverage census, absorbed.
  - Exit: fleet page renders against Shepherd's fleet with `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` unread (network log clean of it when `owner` is configured).
- [ ] **PR 4 — modes + docs**
  - `build-site.mjs` mounts the repo- or fleet-landing per decision 5.
  - README rewrites: claudinite-dashboard (panels, modes, data plane, measured budgets); `docs/skill-usage-metrics/DESIGN.md` updated to the end state (per-repo files are the record, the dashboard is the fleet reader; the fleet aggregate gone). The sheepdog README row goes with the tail's removal PR, not here.

## Execution — runnable in one sitting, no waits

- [ ] Force **usage-fold fleet-wide** (fleet-baseline `follow`, or the scheduler's `wake` per member) so every member's file regenerates at v3 in one pass rather than trickling in over nightly cycles. Exit: every folding member's file reads `version: 3`. (Readers accept v2, so a straggler costs nothing meanwhile.)
- [ ] **Adopt claudinite-dashboard on ClaudiniteCanary** via adopt-pack (no roster → repo mode by shape). Exit: Canary's Pages URL serves the repo dashboard.
- [ ] **Flip Shepherd's declaration**: replace `"rosterFile": "usage-fleet.GENERATED.json"` with `"owner": "missingbulb"` beside its existing excludes. Exit: Shepherd's Pages URL serves the fleet dashboard with no request for `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json`.
- [ ] Verify Shepherd's Pages setting was indeed already on (expected no-op).

## The tail — destructive, only after the cutover is observed working

- [ ] File (do-later, blocked behind PR 3's merge **and** the Shepherd flip) the removal: the `fleet-usage` task, `aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs`, its README + the sheepdog catalog row + the `.gitattributes` entry from the canon; `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` deleted from Shepherd. Filed as work that comes back on its own, never a phase recalled from memory.

## Not in this plan

- Sign-in / GitHub App wiring — #996, #942, #1003.
- Any pre-summed fleet artifact — decision 6's fallback exists only if enumeration measurement forces it.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

# Fleet usage — recompute the fleet-wide skill-usage aggregate

**This task runs no agent.** It is `agent_model: none` with `code-work: node worker.mjs`, so the whole pass is the deterministic [`worker.mjs`](worker.mjs) the executor runs as code-work, which calls its sibling in this folder, the sweep ([`aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs`](aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs)). This file is the human-facing record of what that worker does; there is no agent phase.

## What it does

Daily, over the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` PAT: read this (claudinite-fleet-sheepdog) repo's `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` pack entry `config`, enumerate every repo that owner owns, read each covered member's `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json` at its default branch, and rebuild `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` in this repo on a PR that lands itself where this repo's delivery settings allow (the shared landing helper, `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`).

A **stateless full recompute** — the file is a pure function of the members' current files. Idempotent by definition, self-healing after any past error, and cheap to no-op: a fleet whose numbers did not move produces the same file and opens no PR.

## What it answers that a member cannot

Each member folds its own numbers, so each can say whether a skill ever loads *there*. Whether a skill earns its place at all is a fleet-shaped question: never loading in one repo may only mean it isn't that repo's subject, while never loading in **any** of them means the trigger is mis-described — or that the content should never have been gated behind a skill in the first place. Only a view across every member separates those.

The **conformance checks** are carried at the same grain and for exactly the same reason, and they answer a sharper question, because a check failure is an observed correction rather than an inferred one: the finding went back into the session and the agent fixed it before the work left the branch. A rule with steady failures across the fleet is a guard earning its keep; a rule that has never fired in *any* member is unreachable or describing something that does not happen; a rule firing on nearly every run is a default the corpus should change rather than a violation worth blocking on. The `errors` counter reads differently from all three — enforcement was silently off — and is the one number here whose right value is zero.

The grain is therefore full — week × repo × skill, and week × repo × rule, for history, plus each member's current day window verbatim — with nothing pre-summed. Every coarser view stays derivable from the file; a summary that threw the grain away would not.

A member still on an older fold carries no `checks` key. It lands as an empty check row, never as an exception: the sweep leads the members' upgrades, so that is the normal state for a while.

## Coverage gaps are reported, not skipped

A covered member with no usage file (not folding yet), or one whose file cannot be read, is listed in `coverage.absent` with the reason — census-style. A denominator with an invisible hole in it is worse than no denominator at all.

The `coverage` section accounts for the **whole fleet**, not just the members: uncovered repos land under `coverage.uncovered` and archived/fork/excluded ones under `coverage.outOfScope` (reason inline), neither contributing to any number. The worker also emits a run summary on **every** run — even one that opens no PR — naming every repo under its state, and flagging the folding members with no captured activity that day (*inactive today*). That daily fact lives in the run report, not the file: it moves with the date alone, and the file's unchanged-compare deliberately ignores the day stamp so an unmoved fleet opens no PR.

## A dormant member leaves the denominator

A member that declares `"dormant": true` ([the scheduler's gate](../../../claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)) is dropped from every rate and listed under `coverage.dormant` — distinct from `coverage.absent`, because "not in the race" and "should be folding and isn't" are different facts. Averaging a deliberately silent repo in would drag every fleet-wide number toward zero as the fleet accumulates finished projects. The test is `isDormant`, re-exported from the engine, so the sweep and the member's own scheduler cannot disagree.

## It is a sample, not a census

The file carries a `_note` saying so. Its whole population is *captured* sessions: sessions that merged, plus sessions that ended cleanly enough for the SessionEnd capture to fire. A session whose container was reclaimed, or that crashed, is invisible to every number in it.

The check counts sit inside a narrower boundary still, and the note says that too: they are what a *session* saw. A CI run counts when the session pulled its job log in — which is what "the agent was in the loop on it" means, and it is the loop that produces the correction — while a nightly or post-merge run nobody looked at does not, because nothing was corrected. CI can only see a run that *printed* something, so its share rides separately as `ciRuns`/`ciFailures` rather than skewing a rate. The under-count is one-directional — every check number is a floor on activations, never an over-count — which is what keeps "the checks caught N things fleet-wide this week" a claim worth making.

## Not a fleet mechanism

Its *implementation* reads every repo under the owner, but its declaration, scheduling and lifecycle are those of **any pack task**: it is active because this repo declares the `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` pack, and it runs on this repo's ordinary scheduler. It declares no `fleet` signal and no `fleet` session scope — the cross-repo reach lives in the implementation, never in the wiring.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.

Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. {"number":1158,"title":"claudinite-dashboard: usage-backed data plane, per-repo redesign, repo/fleet modes — and retire fleet-usage","body":"Tracking issue for the dashboard redesign. The plan below is ordered by what blocks (out-of-band setup → one review pass over a PR stack → unattended execution → destructive tail), not by subject. Once agreed, this body is append-only.

## First, the question asked: is `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` redundant?

**Yes — with one catch that sequences the removal.**

- The sweep is a **stateless full recompute, a pure function of the members' current files** (its own README says so). It holds **no longer history** than the members: each member's week rows are append-once and never pruned, so the member files are the complete record and the fleet file adds no depth.
- **Nothing in the canon reads it.** Grep finds only the task's own files, its tests, docs and the `.gitattributes` entry. It was built for fleet-wide analysis by a human/agent reading one file — the fleet dashboard is now that reader, better.
- The **access argument is real and favors dropping**: the aggregate in Shepherd shows anyone with Shepherd read the whole fleet's numbers, while the dashboard reads each member's file *as the viewer* — a repo you can't read renders "not visible to you". Per-repo files are the permission-correct source.
- **Catch 1 — it is currently the fleet dashboard's roster.** Shepherd's declaration reads `"rosterFile": "usage-fleet.GENERATED.json"`. The member list is the one thing genuinely fleet-shaped in it, so the fleet page needs a replacement roster source *before* the file goes (PR 3 below).
- Catch 2 — the `coverage` census (absent / dormant / out-of-scope, with reasons) is the only other content member files can't hold. The fleet page derives it live: a rostered repo with no readable usage file **is** the absent row, and `dormant` is read off the member's own declaration.

So: drop the task and the file — sequenced after the fleet page stops reading it (the tail, below).

## Design decisions

1. **Fresh vs past split.** *Fresh* per page load: repo metadata, head sha, the open-issue page, the runs list — all ETag-revalidated (a 304 is free), target **~5 requests warm, all 304s** on the per-repo page. *Past*: one blob read of `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`, cached by head sha — **zero requests while `main` is unmoved**. Nothing else reaches back in time over the API.
2. **usage.GENERATED.json v3 stays raw data**, not UI-shaped: per-hour and per-day series with per-item detail preserved, so future UI changes re-render without re-folding. Readers accept v2 (legacy at the door): an absent series renders as a stated gap, never a guessed zero — the #1001 rule.
3. **Freshness provenance**: a `generated` stamp in the file, excluded from the worker's unchanged-compare exactly as the fleet file's `generatedAt` already is — so it reads "when the data last moved" and a quiet repo still opens no PR. The head-commit date the page already holds is the upper bound beside it.
4. **usage-fold goes hourly, gated on movement** — signals `commits` + `conversationLogs` + runs movement; a quiet hour declines. The REST-read families stay incremental past their watermarks; day recomputes stay local-git and free.
5. **Mode is structural, no new config key**: a declaration with a roster source (`owner` or legacy `rosterFile`) is a **fleet-dashboard** deployment, anything else is a **repo-dashboard** one; `build-site.mjs` mounts that landing. Nothing to ask at adoption, nothing to misconfigure.
6. **Fleet roster = live enumeration as the viewer**: config `owner` (+ existing `exclude`), membership = a readable `.claudinite-checks.json` at head (sha-cached, so the probe is amortized). This also honors the standing "no repo list exists anywhere in canon code" decision. Fallback if enumeration proves too costly at fleet size: a slim `roster.GENERATED.json` from a Shepherd fleet task (the sanctioned daily auto-merged GENERATED-file shape) — not built unless measurement says so.

## Phase 0 — out-of-band, human

- [ ] Enable **Pages, source "GitHub Actions", on ClaudiniteCanary** — the one repository setting no Action can flip. The adoption run files its own handover issue there with the link; while off, only the deploy job fails. (Shepherd already deploys, so its setting is expected on — verified as an execution step, promoted here only if it turns out off.)

Sign-in for the fleet deployment is already tracked in #996 / #942 / #1003 and blocks nothing here — the token box works today.

## The stack — all code, one review pass, merged base-first

- [ ] **PR 1 — usage-fold v3** (the data plane; everything downstream renders from it)
  - **`hours` tier**, rolling ~72h keyed by UTC hour: counts of scheduler runs / executor runs / agentic runs, plus raw per-run entries (task ids evaluated / executed, which dispatched an agent, conclusion) so the UI can build hover detail. Folded from the Actions runs listing + the run records, incremental past `runsFoldedThrough`. This is the queue-era successor to the dead `tasks` census — closes #994.
  - **day-row additions**: `queue` — closed work items per task × outcome, appended past a watermark (settled data, never re-read); `ruleTokens` — sessions seen + rule tokens summed, parsed from the session-start summary line the capture logs already carry; `linesCommitted` — local git, free; `releases` — tags, one cheap read.
  - **aspirational, resolved inside this PR**: per-session token spend — probe the capture JSONL for usage records; carried if present, otherwise the README names it absent (a stated gap, not an approximation).
  - `generated` stamp per decision 3; `frequency: 'hourly'` + movement precondition per decision 4; README rewritten.
  - Exit: fold runs green on this repo's own logs; a v2 file re-folds to v3 without loss; a quiet-hour run declines.
- [ ] **PR 2 — per-repo page redesign**
  - **At-a-glance tiles**: stars, CI health, waiting-on-a-person minutes (the fleet's flat-rate constant, same published assumption note), "N parked for approval / M for a decision" (the park-kind split `summariseMember` already makes, reused per-repo), open PRs + issues, engine/pack drift vs `canonRepo` (reads *unknown* when unset — never guessed).
  - **One work table** replacing the tasks and queue tables: three views — **stuck / pending / all** — over the union of declared tasks and their items, with view-dependent columns; transitions FLIP-animated (rows enter/leave, columns slide; hand-rolled, the pack keeps zero dependencies). Blocked/parked rows always on top; healthy rows collapsed behind **show all**.
  - **Task execution summary**: per-day stacked outcome bars (the fleet's shape), from the usage `queue` series, today's partial day topped up from the live issue page already fetched.
  - **Scheduler-runs panel condensed to a 48h hourly stacked graph** — scheduler / executor / agentic per hour, hover naming the tasks evaluated / executed / agentic — from the usage `hours` tier, the freshest hours topped up from the runs list already fetched.
  - **Growth block, centrally placed**: 30-day graph, dual axes — rule tokens added to sessions per day, checks executed per day — plus the aspirational series where the file carries them.
  - Exit: cold/warm request counts measured and stated in the README, warm within the ~5-request target.
- [ ] **PR 3 — fleet page from member usage files**
  - Member rows and the activity/growth panels render from each member's usage file (sha-keyed read, zero when unmoved) plus a minimal fresh read per member (ETag'd open-issue page + repo meta), through the existing cache/budget tiers.
  - Roster from `owner` enumeration per decision 6; `rosterFile` still accepted so Shepherd's current declaration keeps working until flipped.
  - A rostered member with no usage file renders **"not folding yet"** — the coverage census, absorbed.
  - Exit: fleet page renders against Shepherd's fleet with `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` unread (network log clean of it when `owner` is configured).
- [ ] **PR 4 — modes + docs**
  - `build-site.mjs` mounts the repo- or fleet-landing per decision 5.
  - README rewrites: claudinite-dashboard (panels, modes, data plane, measured budgets); `docs/skill-usage-metrics/DESIGN.md` updated to the end state (per-repo files are the record, the dashboard is the fleet reader; the fleet aggregate gone). The sheepdog README row goes with the tail's removal PR, not here.

## Execution — runnable in one sitting, no waits

- [ ] Force **usage-fold fleet-wide** (fleet-baseline `follow`, or the scheduler's `wake` per member) so every member's file regenerates at v3 in one pass rather than trickling in over nightly cycles. Exit: every folding member's file reads `version: 3`. (Readers accept v2, so a straggler costs nothing meanwhile.)
- [ ] **Adopt claudinite-dashboard on ClaudiniteCanary** via adopt-pack (no roster → repo mode by shape). Exit: Canary's Pages URL serves the repo dashboard.
- [ ] **Flip Shepherd's declaration**: replace `"rosterFile": "usage-fleet.GENERATED.json"` with `"owner": "missingbulb"` beside its existing excludes. Exit: Shepherd's Pages URL serves the fleet dashboard with no request for `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json`.
- [ ] Verify Shepherd's Pages setting was indeed already on (expected no-op).

## The tail — destructive, only after the cutover is observed working

- [ ] File (do-later, blocked behind PR 3's merge **and** the Shepherd flip) the removal: the `fleet-usage` task, `aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs`, its README + the sheepdog catalog row + the `.gitattributes` entry from the canon; `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` deleted from Shepherd. Filed as work that comes back on its own, never a phase recalled from memory.

## Not in this plan

- Sign-in / GitHub App wiring — #996, #942, #1003.

  - **One work table** replacing the tasks and queue tables: three views — **stuck / pending / all** — over the union of declared tasks and their items, with view-dependent columns; transitions FLIP-animated (rows enter/leave, columns slide; hand-rolled, the pack keeps zero dependencies). Blocked/parked rows always on top; healthy rows collapsed behind **show all**.
  - **Task execution summary**: per-day stacked outcome bars (the fleet's shape), from the usage `queue` series, today's partial day topped up from the live issue page already fetched.
  - **Scheduler-runs panel condensed to a 48h hourly stacked graph** — scheduler / executor / agentic per hour, hover naming the tasks evaluated / executed / agentic — from the usage `hours` tier, the freshest hours topped up from the runs list already fetched.
  - **Growth block, centrally placed**: 30-day graph, dual axes — rule tokens added to sessions per day, checks executed per day — plus the aspirational series where the file carries them.
  - Exit: cold/warm request counts measured and stated in the README, warm within the ~5-request target.
- [ ] **PR 3 — fleet page from member usage files**
  - Member rows and the activity/growth panels render from each member's usage file (sha-keyed read, zero when unmoved) plus a minimal fresh read per member (ETag'd open-issue page + repo meta), through the existing cache/budget tiers.
  - Roster from `owner` enumeration per decision 6; `rosterFile` still accepted so Shepherd's current declaration keeps working until flipped.
  - A rostered member with no usage file renders **"not folding yet"** — the coverage census, absorbed.
  - Exit: fleet page renders against Shepherd's fleet with `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` unread (network log clean of it when `owner` is configured).
- [ ] **PR 4 — modes + docs**
  - `build-site.mjs` mounts the repo- or fleet-landing per decision 5.
  - README rewrites: claudinite-dashboard (panels, modes, data plane, measured budgets); `docs/skill-usage-metrics/DESIGN.md` updated to the end state (per-repo files are the record, the dashboard is the fleet reader; the fleet aggregate gone). The sheepdog README row goes with the tail's removal PR, not here.

## Execution — runnable in one sitting, no waits

- [ ] Force **usage-fold fleet-wide** (fleet-baseline `follow`, or the scheduler's `wake` per member) so every member's file regenerates at v3 in one pass rather than trickling in over nightly cycles. Exit: every folding member's file reads `version: 3`. (Readers accept v2, so a straggler costs nothing meanwhile.)
- [ ] **Adopt claudinite-dashboard on ClaudiniteCanary** via adopt-pack (no roster → repo mode by shape). Exit: Canary's Pages URL serves the repo dashboard.
- [ ] **Flip Shepherd's declaration**: replace `"rosterFile": "usage-fleet.GENERATED.json"` with `"owner": "missingbulb"` beside its existing excludes. Exit: Shepherd's Pages URL serves the fleet dashboard with no request for `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json`.
- [ ] Verify Shepherd's Pages setting was indeed already on (expected no-op).

## The tail — destructive, only after the cutover is observed working

- [ ] File (do-later, blocked behind PR 3's merge **and** the Shepherd flip) the removal: the `fleet-usage` task, `aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs`, its README + the sheepdog catalog row + the `.gitattributes` entry from the canon; `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` deleted from Shepherd. Filed as work that comes back on its own, never a phase recalled from memory.

file.content:
Fleet status

How this reads your repo

Everything happens in this browser tab. The page calls api.github.com directly as you, so your own GitHub permissions are the only access control — there is no backend, no shared credential, and this page can show you nothing your account cannot already read. Your credential is held for this tab only (sessionStorage) and is sent to GitHub and nowhere else.

Where sign-in is configured, Sign in with GitHub authorizes once and everything afterwards runs as you. Otherwise the page falls back to a pasted token, which needs read-only Contents, Issues and Actions.

Responses are cached in this browser: repo content is keyed by commit SHA, live data is revalidated with ETags (a 304 costs no rate limit), settled history ages out after 24 hours, and a member's commit graph — the one read here that is decoration rather than a fault signal — after six, and not at all when the budget is tight. Clear cache forces a cold read. Pass ?repo=owner/name to jump straight to a repo.

What Claudinite did for this fleet this week

The work the machinery did that nobody had to do — in a window, this week against last, because a total that only ever grows tells you nothing about today. Every figure is a count of things that individually happened, from reads this page already makes. There is no estimate of hours saved and no score: nothing here measures those, so nothing here claims them.

Fleet at a glance

Each tile counts members, never things. "47 open items" is not a number anyone acts on; "3 members need you" is — it is the length of this morning's list. A tile is coloured only when it is reporting something, so a coloured tile always means look here.

The last two mornings

The fleet's own morning brief — what the fleet accomplished that day, and the project worth returning to — written by the digest task into the enforcer repo, one file per day. A day with no brief is a normal state: the task had nothing to report, or has not run yet. Both files are content at a path, so a warm load costs nothing to show them.

Fleet activity

Every other panel here answers where do I need to look, and after a good week they are all zero — which is exactly what a dead fleet looks like too. This is the other reading: what happened, per day. Every figure comes from reads the page already makes, so the panel costs no extra request; what that costs instead is depth, and where a series runs past what one page of issues or thirty runs can see it says so rather than drawing a confident zero.

Members — worst first

Ordered by the worst thing that is true of each member, not by how much it has. One item parked for a human outranks forty healthy ones, because the first needs you today and the second is the system working. A member that cannot be read, one that does not run Claudinite, and one that is fine are three different rows and never collapse into a zero.

The columns are grouped as three questions, in the order you ask them: Activity — is anyone working on this repo; Waiting on a person — what is on your plate here and roughly how long it is; Claudinite — what the machinery is doing. Stars and CI sit beside the name rather than in columns, because they are how you recognise the row rather than findings about it. Every column but the commit curve comes from a read this page already makes, which is also why four things are missing: rule tokens, test counts and time saved would each need a member's own files read, and conversation-log sessions a branch listing. Issues and pull requests are counted within the issue window — the most recent hundred — so an older one is not counted rather than counted wrongly.

Commits is the last 90 days as a curve, drawn by week — a quarter at daily resolution is a sawtooth of weekends and Tuesdays with no shape to read — and scaled to that row's own busiest week, so height compares two weeks in one repo and never two repos. The number beneath is the real total, and the hover carries both peaks. A break in the curve is a stretch outside the year GitHub reports statistics for, which is not the same as a quiet one; a cell reading not read is this page declining to spend the request, since this is the one figure here that is decoration rather than a fault signal and so the first thing a tight budget goes without.

Est. is a deliberately crude figure: every item parked for a person, at a flat 7 minutes each. Nothing here measures how long a park actually takes, and the honest way to publish a number nothing measures is to publish the assumption where you can argue with it. A broken scheduler is not counted into it — that is not a queue of work to get through — though it is still reported. Packs wears the mount's verdict as a badge: a scheduler run when what is declared here is current, a timer when it is behind, and the versions on hover. Two facts read together, and the second says the same thing on nearly every row, so it earns a corner rather than a column.

Click a member to open its scheduler in full.

Tasks across the fleet

The one question no single repo's page can answer. A task ships from a shared pack, so it runs in every member that declares it — and the same task parked in four members at once is a canon problem, while in any one repo it looks like that repo's bad luck.

A shared pack's task, everywhere it runs. One parked in several members at once is the pack's problem, not any one member's.

Pack adoption

Who a change to a pack would reach. Before editing a pack's rules or its checks, this is the blast radius; after, it is how many members have to converge before the change is real.

This repo at a glance

Parked and past a leash are the two that mean work has stopped: the first is waiting on a person, the second has been sitting in a machine state longer than its cadence allows. The rest are context for reading those two.

Task roster — every declared task

Every declared task gets a row, including one that has never run — which is usually the thing you opened this for. A list derived from the work items would omit it silently, and a task that never fired looks identical to one that has nothing to do.

done delivered obsolete no outcome

Queue — open work items

One open issue per piece of scheduled work, labelled with the state it is in. Idle is how long it has sat in that state: a long idle in a machine state is the queue stuck, and a long idle in needs human is you.

Scheduler runs

The Actions runs behind the queue. A run that fails is not the same as a task that fails — the first means the scheduler never got to decide anything, which is why a member whose runs are red reads as broken even when every task looks healthy.

1	// claudinite-dashboard — a browser view of what a repo's (or a fleet's) Claudinite
2	// scheduler is doing, published as a static site.
3	//
4	// WHY A PACK AND NOT ENGINE CODE. The dashboard is not part of running the scheduler:
5	// nothing converges, scheduler runs or executes because it exists, and a member that never
6	// looks at it should not carry it. Engine code is what every member runs; this is
7	// content a member OPTS INTO, and adoptable content in this corpus is a pack. That
8	// also buys it the things a pack has and engine code does not — its own version and
9	// migration lane, a declaration that gates it, and an adoption moment at which its
10	// deployment can be wired.
11	//
12	// WHAT IT READS. Only the queue's own vocabulary and the task declarations at HEAD,
13	// through the engine modules that define them (`../../engine/scheduler/queue/*`), so
14	// the page cannot drift from the mechanism it renders. Those relative paths resolve
15	// identically in the canon (`packs/<id>/` beside `engine/`) and in a member's mount
16	// (`.claudinite/shared/packs/<id>/` beside `.claudinite/shared/engine/`), which is
17	// why the pack can be read straight out of the mount with nothing rewritten.
18	//
19	// NO PROSE. There is no way to write the dashboard wrongly in a consuming repo — it is
20	// a page, not a practice — and prose here would cost every session in every declaring
21	// repo tokens for something no session acts on. Its README carries the explanation
22	// instead and `prose` stays null.
23	//
24	// TWO CHECKS, AND A TASK, ALL THE DIGEST'S. `tasks/fleet-digest/` writes the fleet's
25	// dated morning brief that the fleet page reads (it moved here from the `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`
26	// pack, which enumerated the fleet but never showed anyone the result). Its two checks
27	// live in its own folder because nothing else reads them: `digest-plain-text` holds the
28	// landed briefs to plain text — they are sent verbatim through a renderer that neither
29	// parses markdown nor keeps line breaks — and `dated-fixture-collision` keeps the
30	// task's own test fixtures out of the year range the fleet writes real briefs in.
31	//
32	// THE TASK IS NOT GATED, and that is the cost of declaring this pack: a repo that wants
33	// only the page gets the digest task too, and the task needs `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` to
34	// read every repo under the owner. Without that secret the executor parks its item
35	// asking for one. The README says so where someone deciding to adopt will read it.
36	//
37	// PUBLISHING IS THE ADOPTION MOMENT. `.github/workflows/` is the one directory the
38	// nightly update can never push to (the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is refused there), so
39	// a deploy workflow can only arrive by being SEEDED — written by the install flow and
40	// committed by the adopting session, which holds a credential the Action does not.
41	// Hence the `seedOps` entry: adopting the pack is what wires the Pages deploy, and
42	// the workflow is the member's from the moment it lands.
43	//
44	// THE BUILD SCRIPT DELIBERATELY IS NOT SEEDED. `build-site.mjs` lives in the pack and
45	// is read out of the mount by the seeded workflow, exactly as the scheduler stub reads
46	// the engine's scheduler run. So the assembly logic keeps converging with the canon while the
47	// workflow — the part that cannot converge — stays a one-time seed. Only the file that
48	// has to be frozen is frozen.
49	import datedFixtureCollision from './tasks/fleet-digest/dated-fixture-collision.mjs';
50	import digestPlainText from './tasks/fleet-digest/digest-plain-text.mjs';
51	import { fleetTokenHandoverStep } from './tasks/fleet-digest/fleet-token.mjs';
52	
53	export default {

2	// (skill-usage-metrics DESIGN §4.2), and the parsers that read them back.
3	//
4	// TWO FAMILIES, ONE OF THEM HISTORICAL. `claudinite-task-run` was the SLOT
5	// scheduler's own line, one per due task per run; the slot scheduler is retired
6	// (#974) and nothing writes that line any more. The parser stays, and only the
7	// parser: Actions logs from before the retirement are still inside their retention
8	// window, and the usage fold still counts them. Nothing new should be taught this
9	// shape — `claudinite-task-exec` below is the live record.
10	//
11	// The counts these produce are exact within the Actions log retention window, and
12	// that is worth stating next to the capture-derived counts they land beside.
13	
14	// The five things a slot scheduler run could do with a due task. One name per
15	// outcome, used verbatim as the counter key in the aggregate, so there is no
16	// mapping table between "what the run said" and "what the fold counted" to drift.
17	export const TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES = Object.freeze([
18	  // A dispatch issue was filed: an agent session ran this task.
19	  'agent',
20	  // The task ran with NO agent — an `agent_model: none` task (code-work is the
21	  // whole task), or an agentful one whose code-work requested no agent phase.
22	  // Kebab, not the declaration field's `code_work`: this word is a WIRE token,
23	  // constrained to the line format's `[a-z-]+` charset.
24	  'code-work',
25	  // Due, but its precondition said there was nothing to do.
26	  'skipped',
27	  // Its code-work failed; the run converged the task to a needs-human issue.
28	  'failed',
29	  // Due and past its precondition, but no NEW agent run started: this slot was
30	  // already dispatched (exactly-once), an earlier dispatch is still open
31	  // (at-most-one-open), or another task claimed the run exclusively. Work that
32	  // was wanted and did not happen this run.
33	  'deferred',
34	]);
35	
36	// An empty per-task counter row — every outcome present, zeros included, so a row's
37	// shape never depends on which outcomes a task happened to hit.
38	export const emptyTaskRun = () => Object.fromEntries(TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES.map((o) => [o, 0]));
39	
40	// The line format. `v1` is the shape's version: a reader that meets a `v2` line
41	// knows it is looking at something it was not written for, instead of silently
42	// half-parsing it.
43	export const TASK_RUN_TAG = 'claudinite-task-run';
44	const VERSION = 'v1';
45	
46	// Actions stamps every log line with its own timestamp before the command's output,
47	// so the parse tolerates that prefix — without it, a fetched log reads as having
48	// printed nothing at all.
49	const LINE_RE = new RegExp(
50	  String.raw`^(?:\S+\s+)?${TASK_RUN_TAG} ${VERSION} (\S+)/(\S+) \[(\S+)\] ([a-z-]+)\s*$`,
51	);
52	
53	// One line → `{ pack, task, slotId, outcome }`, or null for anything that is not a
54	// record of this version. Deliberately strict: an unknown outcome word is NOT a
55	// record, because counting it would mint a counter key nothing ever reads.
56	// The code phase has been renamed twice, and job logs outlive both renames:
57	// `preprocess` (pre-2026-08-06) and `prework` (pre-2026-08-18) are the earlier
58	// words for what is now `code-work`. Runs logged under either still parse, each
59	// normalized straight to the canonical word.
60	// Exported because the outcome words are also the usage aggregate's counter KEYS,
61	// and that file holds rows written under the older words. Its decode renames them
62	// by this same map, so a rename never silently drops a historical count.
63	export const LEGACY_TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES = Object.freeze({ preprocess: 'code-work', prework: 'code-work' });
64	
65	export function parseTaskRun(line) {
66	  const m = LINE_RE.exec(line);
67	  if (!m) return null;
68	  const [, pack, task, slotId, word] = m;
69	  const outcome = LEGACY_TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES[word] ?? word;
70	  if (!TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES.includes(outcome)) return null;
71	  return { pack, task, slotId, outcome };
72	}

74	// Every record in one job log. The log is the whole job's output — this picks its
75	// own lines out of it and ignores everything else.
76	export function parseTaskRuns(text) {
77	  const out = [];
78	  for (const line of String(text ?? '').split('\n')) {
79	    const rec = parseTaskRun(line);
80	    if (rec) out.push(rec);
81	  }
82	  return out;

88	// (resolve-dispatch on a terminal verdict, record-exec.mjs at convergence), they

94	export const TASK_EXEC_STATUSES = Object.freeze([
95	  // The dispatch ran to completion within its ceiling; the issue was closed.
96	  'success',
97	  // The run failed (task failure or ceiling violation); converged to needs-human.
98	  'failed',
99	  // The dispatch named a task the repo no longer carries (file gone, pack

101	  'task-gone',
102	  // The dispatch was malformed (bad path shape, unparseable declaration) and was
103	  // converged to needs-human without running.
104	  'invalid',
105	]);
106	
107	export const TASK_EXEC_TAG = 'claudinite-task-exec';
108	
109	// The bracketed field is the OCCURRENCE'S IDENTITY, which is a different thing under
110	// each dispatch mechanism: a slot id (`d2026-08-06`) where slots decide what runs, and
111	// the work item's issue number (`#867`) where the queue does. `slotId` keeps its name
112	// for the fielded records that already carry one; what it must never become is a
113	// constant, since it is the only join from a record back to the work it describes.
114	export const renderTaskExec = ({ pack, task, slotId, status }) =>
115	  `${TASK_EXEC_TAG} ${VERSION} ${pack}/${task} [${slotId ?? 'unknown'}] ${status}`;
116	
117	const EXEC_LINE_RE = new RegExp(
118	  String.raw`(?:^|\s)${TASK_EXEC_TAG} ${VERSION} (\S+)/(\S+) \[(\S+)\] ([a-z-]+)\s*$`,
119	);
120	
121	export function parseTaskExec(line) {
122	  const m = EXEC_LINE_RE.exec(line);
123	  if (!m) return null;
124	  const [, pack, task, slotId, status] = m;
125	  if (!TASK_EXEC_STATUSES.includes(status)) return null;
126	  return { pack, task, slotId, status };
127	}
128	
129	export function parseTaskExecs(text) {
