content.text:
Both answers below; the second needed measuring rather than guessing, so I did that first.

## Is the signal collection expensive?

**It doesn't run every run.** `evaluate(task)` fires only when a task has no open standing item **and** its most recent anchor isn't already covered **and** the schedule board doesn't already record a decline at that anchor ([`scheduler-run.mjs:124-183`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs#L124)). So it's one collection **per uncovered anchor**, not per task per run. A repo whose tasks all hold standing items makes no signal calls at all. The executor collects a second time at pick — but only for an item that was actually created.

Measured on this repo (54 commits over the last two days, ~27/day):

| | calls per evaluation | how often |
|---|---|---|
| `usage-fold` (hourly, 2h window) | 1 commit list + 1 detail **per commit** (median 2, p90 5, max 9) + 2 for the logs branch → **~5 median, ~12 worst** | 24×/day |
| a daily task with `commits` (25h window) | ~34 commits in the window → **~35 calls** | 1×/day each |

Wall clock, from the last 30 real scheduler runs: **25–68 s, median ~32 s** for the *whole* run — checkout, node, queue read, board, signals. Collection is a fraction of that; the per-commit loop is serial, so it's the only part that grows.

**Processing power: negligible.** Regexes over commit metadata and filenames. The genuinely heavy work in this pipeline isn't a signal at all — it's the fold worker reading every capture blob, and that runs as code-work.

**Tokens: zero.** Signal collection is engine code inside the Action; no model is involved. And `usage-fold` is `agent_model: 'none'`, so making it hourly added **no model tokens whatsoever** — only API calls.

Against budget: `GITHUB_TOKEN` in Actions is documented at 1,000 requests/hour per repository, so usage-fold's ~5/hour is well under 1%. *Caveat: I could not re-verify that figure from this sandbox — the proxy blocks the docs — so treat the 1,000 as recalled, not checked.*

**The one thing worth flagging, and it predates this change:** `windowCommits` makes **one detail read per commit** to get its changed-file list, and two tasks that both declare `commits` each pay their own window read — there's no cross-task sharing, because each task's window is its own frequency. On a repo at 27 commits/day the *daily* tasks dominate the whole signal layer, not the hourly one. `/compare/{base}...{head}` would return commits and files in one call, but it gives an **aggregate** file list, and `isSubstantive`'s corpus-only exclusion needs the per-commit pairing — so it is not a drop-in swap. Noted, not attempted.

## Does the design doc collapse?

Yes — and it collapses into **three** places, not two. I inventoried all 769 lines:

| § | lines | already lives, or belongs |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 placement, sources | 34 | canon rules that already exist ("the canon knows mechanisms, never repos") |
| 3.x capture | ~100 | `capture-log.mjs` / `session-end.mjs` headers + claudinite-growth's README |
| 4.1 check activations | 101 | **already re-stated nearly verbatim** in usage-fold's README and `fold-usage.mjs`'s header |
| 4.2–4.3 the census | 85 | usage-fold README's "What each occurrence came to" |
| 5 + shape | 146 | usage-fold README + `usage-format.mjs` header |
| 6 fleet aggregate | 63 | superseded; dies with [#1166](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1166) |
| 7 consumers | 40 | split — the reader half is the **dashboard** README, the promotion-ladder half is canon-curation's |
| 8–9 TTLs, failure modes | 57 | usage-fold README |
| 10 + two owner rounds | 57 | **the residue with no other home** — recorded owner decisions, which by this repo's own convention belong in the local pack's *Standing owner decisions*, not a `docs/` file |

So your instinct matches a rule already on the books: behaviour belongs in the module header and the pack README. Most of §4–5 got rewritten into usage-fold's README during this change anyway, which is exactly why the duplication is now visible.

The cost of doing it: eight module headers cite it by section (`skill-usage-metrics DESIGN §4.2`), and nothing checks those — the same class as the stale `doc:` pointers in #975.

Given [#1165](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1165) is green and awaiting your review, I'd rather not fold a 769-line redistribution into it.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## The conversation lifecycle — capture in-session, extract in the daily task, retention

The pack also owns **extraction from working sessions**, replacing the old in-session post-merge
lessons pass. Capture and extraction split by what each needs: **capture** needs the live session
transcript, so it runs in-session (at merge, and again when the session ends); **extraction** only
reads the already-pushed logs, so it is the conversation half of the ordinary `growth-extract`
scheduled task — the logs branch is *in the repo*, so reading it, committing lessons to local packs,
and pruning are plain local git on the working tree; only posting the summary on the issue uses the
GitHub MCP tools.

1. **Capture — a step in the merge-to-main skill** (in-session, where the transcript lives).
   Right after a merge lands:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo itself: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`).
   Deterministic, seconds; it bundles the session transcript (sidechains inline, timestamp
   order), **scrubs enumeration-first** (every value the environment holds — `process.env`
   minus a short named allowlist of structural values, plus known credential stores — is
   redacted wherever it appears, with credential-shape patterns as the backstop; a secret the
   applies the [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) skill (the
   friction signals and the measured efficiency analysis, computable from the log's timestamps and
   token usage) over [extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)'s shared bar, routes keepers into
   the member's local packs, and posts on the worked issue, for each rule that landed, a
   **200-word-max** summary of the slice of conversation that caused it — the dialogue itself is
   never pasted there, it is far too verbose for an issue —
   **extraction is the only path to permanence**: a log that yields no rule gets no comment,
   and its conversation is gone once retention deletes it (a deliberate owner call).
3. **Deletion — the agentless `logs-prune` task**
   ([tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs](tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs)), daily, over the same branch: every
   capture past `config.retention_days` is removed, on the stamp in its filename alone. What makes
   that safe without an agent is the reading window above — the extract run reads from the oldest end
   of the branch on every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. **Unset retention = the
   prune deletes nothing** (capture-only, fail-safe).

No adoption question over it — `retention_days` stays unset (hidden) by default, which is
fail-safe (capture-only). A project that wants the prune active sets `config.retention_days`
itself (10 is the recommended floor); nothing else to schedule, since both tasks ride the
fleet's one daily run like the other growth tasks.

## Skill-usage metrics — what the mounted skills actually do

Mounting a skill only puts its name and one-line description into the session prompt; whether the
model ever **loads** it is discretion, and nothing recorded it. So the promotion ladder's
skill-vs-prose call had no empirical feedback: a skill whose trigger never fires looked exactly like
one that fires daily, and a "skill" that loads in every session (rules wearing a skill's clothes)
looked exactly like a genuinely activity-scoped one.

The [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/README.md) task closes that loop — hourly, agentless, seconds. It
counts skill loads **and their denominators** (captures, merges, sessions, user messages, user
commands) out of the logs this pack already captures, into

input.title: Dissolve docs/skill-usage-metrics/DESIGN.md into the packs that own its subjects
input.body:
The owner's read, and it holds up against the tree: this design doc collapses into the pack that collects the signals and into the dashboard. It is 769 lines describing a pipeline that is now built, and the canon's own rule for that is already written — *behaviour belongs in the module header and the pack README*, not in a doc that has to be kept in step with both.

The evidence, section by section (line counts from `2026-08-21`):

| § | Lines | Where it already lives, or should |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Where knowledge lives | 16 | A standing architectural rule ("the canon knows mechanisms, never repos") — belongs with the local pack's standing decisions, not in one initiative's doc |
| 2 Sources of truth | 18 | `claudinite-growth/README.md` |
| 3 Capture (3.1–3.5) | ~100 | `claudinite-growth/README.md` already carries the capture lifecycle and retention almost verbatim; `capture-log.mjs`'s header carries the rest. **§3.4 (capturing an unattended session, where no SessionEnd hook fires) and §3.5 (the ordering constraint) are the one part with no other home** — they go into the pack README beside the lifecycle they belong to |
| 4.1 Check activations | 101 | Duplicated: `usage-fold/README.md`'s "The check failures are the win" and `fold-usage.mjs`'s header both carry the three marks, the CI-in-the-loop rule and the floor property |
| 4.2 Task invocations | 69 | Describes the retired slot-scheduler census. Keep two sentences of it as history in `usage-fold/README.md` (which already has them) and drop the rest |
| 4.3 Exec statuses | 16 | `usage-fold/README.md` |
| 5 The per-repo aggregate + shape | 146 | Duplicated: `usage-fold/README.md` and `usage-format.mjs`'s header |
| 6 The fleet aggregate | 63 | Superseded; **deleted outright** — the task it describes goes in #1166 |
| 7 Consumers | 40 | Split: the promotion-ladder half to `claudinite-growth/README.md`, the reader half to `claudinite-dashboard/README.md` |
| 8 TTLs | 12 | `claudinite-growth/README.md` (it already states retention) |
| 9 Failure modes | 45 | Duplicated: `usage-fold/README.md`'s "Failure is visible, never silent" |
| 10 + the two later rounds | 57 | Owner decisions with their rationale. These are the doc's only irreplaceable content — move them to the local pack's standing decisions, where a session actually reads them |

So the shape of the change: **almost nothing is written fresh.** Two sections move (§3.4/§3.5, and the decision record), one is deleted, and the rest is verified as already-covered and then dropped. If a section turns out *not* to be covered where this table claims, write it into the pack — do not keep the doc alive for it.

## The references are the real work

Eight files point into this doc by section number, and a dangling `§` pointer is worse than no pointer:

```
engine/hooks/session-end-command.mjs          §3.3
engine/scheduler/run-record.mjs               §4.2
packs/claudinite-growth/session-end.mjs       (unnumbered)
packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/usage-fold/task.mjs        §5
packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/usage-fold/worker.mjs      §5
packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/usage-fold/fold-usage.mjs  §4, §5
docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md         §4.2 and one unnumbered
```

Each becomes either a pointer to the pack README section that absorbed it, or — better where the sentence was only citing itself — nothing at all. Use the `repo-text-sweeps` skill; grep for `skill-usage-metrics` afterwards and confirm zero hits outside history.

## Done looks like

`docs/skill-usage-metrics/` is gone; no file in the tree references it; the owner decision record is in the local pack's standing decisions; §3.4 and §3.5's content is in `claudinite-growth/README.md`; the full suite and `check_the_world` are green.

## Worth deciding while doing it

The same argument applies to the other five `docs/*/DESIGN.md` — `tasks-dispatch` alone is 1,958 lines and is cited from dozens of module headers. **Do not sweep them in this change.** If the pattern holds, say so in a comment here and let the owner decide separately; a 4,300-line doc migration is not something to discover mid-run.

**Your read holds up.** Of 769 lines: §4.1, §5 and §9 are near-verbatim duplicates of what `usage-fold/README.md` and the module headers already say; §3 is duplicated by the growth README's capture lifecycle; §4.2 describes the retired slot-scheduler census; §6 is superseded by this PR. Only two things have no other home — §3.4/§3.5 (capturing an unattended session, and the ordering constraint) and the owner decision record. The issue tables that out section by section, so the run verifies rather than rewrites.

---

**Is the signals collection expensive? Measured, not estimated — and the answer is no, with one pre-existing cost worth knowing about.**

The premise that it runs "every run" is the part to correct. `evaluate(task)` fires only when a task has **no open standing item**, its most recent anchor is **uncovered**, and the schedule board doesn't already record a decline at that anchor (`scheduler-run.mjs:124-190`). So collection is **once per uncovered anchor per task**, not once per run. A repo whose tasks all have standing items makes zero signal calls.

Measured on this repo:

| | Measured |
|---|---|
| Scheduler run, wall clock (last 30 runs) | **25–68 s**, median ~32 s — that's the whole run: checkout, node, queue read, board, signals |
| Commits in `usage-fold`'s 2 h window | median **2**, p90 5, max 9 |
| Commits in a daily task's 25 h window | **34** |

Per collector, per evaluation: `conversationLogs` is **exactly 2 calls** (branch + tree) and a regex over filenames — the tree is one call whatever the branch holds. `commits` is `1 + N`, because `windowCommits` reads each commit's detail for its file list. So hourly `usage-fold` costs **~5 calls median, ~12 worst case**, ≈120/day — against the ~1,000/hour per-repository ceiling for `GITHUB_TOKEN` in Actions. (That ceiling is from memory; the sandbox proxy blocks GitHub's docs, so I could not re-verify it here.)

**Processing power: negligible** — regexes over commit metadata and filenames. The heavy work in this pipeline is elsewhere: the fold *worker* reading every capture blob (256 MB buffer), which is code-work, not a signal.

**Tokens: zero.** Signal collection is engine code inside the Action; no model is involved. And `usage-fold` is `agent_model: 'none'`, so making it hourly added **no model tokens at all** — only those ~5 API calls an hour.

**The one thing worth flagging** is the pre-existing `1 + N` shape. On a repo doing 34 commits/day, each daily task declaring `commits` pays ~35 serial calls, and two such tasks don't share the read — each has its own window. `GET /compare/{base}...{head}` returns commits *and* files in one call, but only an aggregate file list, which breaks `isSubstantive`'s per-commit corpus-only test. So it isn't a swap I'd make without proving behaviour identical, and the canon's own rule says prove it or leave it alone. Say the word and I'll file it.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

input.commit_title: claudinite-dashboard: a usage-backed data plane, the repo page rebuilt, and repo/fleet modes (#1165)
input.commit_message:
Refs #1158.

The page reads two kinds of data and treats them differently: what is true now
is a handful of ETag-revalidated live reads, what happened before is one
sha-keyed read of the repo's own usage.GENERATED.json. Measured: 14 requests
cold, 5 warm and every one of them a free 304.

usage-fold becomes that past-data plane — hourly on a movement precondition,
with an hour tier, the queue's own closed items in place of the retired
slot-scheduler census (#994), rule tokens, token spend, git and release series,
and a freshness stamp excluded from the unchanged-compare.

The repo page gains at-a-glance tiles and one work table with three views in
place of the roster and queue tables; the fleet page reads each member's usage
file and enumerates its roster from an owner as the viewer rather than from a
stored list. Which dashboard a deployment builds is decided by its config's
shape.

Absent sources leave no key rather than a zero throughout, and every panel keeps
"not read" and "nothing happened" apart.
